transcript.en: And then, of course, the most important impact, for me, is kind of for patients. Populations everywhere are the same, everyone is suffering from disease and illness.
transcript.zh: 当然，对我来说最重要的影响还是在于患者。各地的民众都是一样的，每个人都在遭受疾病和伤痛的折磨。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And if these acts might mean, in the future, that a Chinese drug is not allowed into the US because of political reasons, and that means a US patient can't get access to the life-saving drug they need in their own home country, what does that mean?
transcript.zh: 如果这些法案意味着，未来一款中国药物仅仅因为政治原因而无法进入美国，进而导致美国患者在自己的国家无法获得所需的救命药，那意味着什么？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: It might mean they're going to travel to another country to get access to that care. And to be honest, we're seeing that already today. There was an article in the Wall Street Journal a few days ago about medical tourism into China.
transcript.zh: 这可能意味着他们不得不远赴他国去寻求这种治疗。老实说，我们现在就已经看到这种苗头了。《华尔街日报》几天前就发表过一篇关于前往中国进行医疗旅游的报道。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: I mean, not because of what we're talking about, not because of these political reasons, but because China is producing really good healthcare that even Americans are willing to travel to to get. And we might see that trend increasing as different types of pressures are impacting US healthcare.
transcript.zh: 我的意思是，那倒不是因为我们刚才讨论的那些政治原因，而是因为中国正在提供非常优质的医疗服务，连美国人都愿意专程前往就医。随着各种压力对美国医疗体系产生冲击，我们可能会看到这种趋势进一步加剧。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Ruby, I want to talk about the digital system, because you spend quite a bit of your book talking about this. You've practiced in the NHS, obviously; you've worked inside a Chinese health platform. Take me through the state of digitization in three systems: in Britain, in the US, where you've spent some time, and in China. What's each getting right, and where does each seem to get stuck?
transcript.zh: Ruby，我想聊聊数字化系统，因为你在书中花了不少篇幅讨论这个问题。你显然在英国 NHS 工作过，也在中国的医疗平台任职过。请为我梳理一下这三个体系的数字化现状：英国、你待过一段时间的美国，以及中国。各自做对了什么，又都在哪里卡了壳？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Maybe I'll start at home, so here in the UK. The NHS is really struggling to digitize. I think there's been a lot of good work done, but it's sort of, if you're trying to add on new shiny tools and clamp them to the side of a very rusty machine, then how far are you going to be able to get?
transcript.zh: 也许我可以先从英国本地谈起。NHS 在数字化转型方面步履维艰。我认为这里面已经做了不少扎实的工作，但这有点像：如果你试图把崭新光鲜的工具硬生生拼接到一台锈迹斑斑的老机器上，你究竟能走多远？

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Yeah, so it's a really basic problem. It's the machine itself. It's the infrastructure that's really lacking.
transcript.zh: 是的，所以这是个很基础的问题。问题出在机器本身，真正匮乏的是基础设施。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah, the infrastructure. How can you take it aside, break it down, and make it better? It's really, really difficult to do. Not to mention the fact that the NHS is a mostly public system model.
transcript.zh: 对，基础设施。你怎么可能把它拆开、分解然后再重新优化？这真的非常非常难做。更不用提 NHS 基本上是一个公立医疗体系模型了。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And so who is going to fund these innovative changes when you've got disease and death happening? The argument for injecting capital into the right parts of healthcare to make the necessary system changes is very difficult. There's lots of bureaucracy.
transcript.zh: 面对眼前不断的疾病与死亡，谁又来为这些创新变革买单呢？要主张把资金注入医疗体系的关键环节以完成必要的系统性改革，是非常困难的。体制内存在着繁文缛节。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: The way the system is set up, it's very difficult to pilot digital tools at local level and then scale them. You have to do different contracts with different people. It's very, very complicated.
transcript.zh: 按照目前的体系架构，很难在地方层面试点数字化工具并予以规模化推广。你必须跟形形色色的人签不同的合同，情况极其复杂。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And that means that even though the digital health innovation ecosystem, because the UK's kind of science talent, the legacy of it is still so strong, you have a lot of cool stuff being built here, but then they go elsewhere because they can't grow. And so that takes us to the US system, where it's very...
transcript.zh: 这意味着，尽管数字医疗创新生态方面——英国由于雄厚的科研人才储备和历史底蕴——诞生了许多非常酷的技术，但由于无法在此壮大，它们最终都流向了他国。这也就引出了美国体系，在那里情况截然...

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: balanced. It's a very capitalist health system, which is certainly not a model that the rest of the world is looking to, you know, take on. But it works very well for the private sector actors that want to make money from it.
transcript.zh: 平衡。它是一个高度资本主义化的医疗体系，这绝对不是世界其他地方想要借鉴的模式。但对于那些想从中赚钱的私营部门参与者来说，它运转得非常好。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: No, indeed.
transcript.zh: 确实如此。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: People pay out of pocket exorbitant costs. You have private hospital chains. A digital health company can go to the US from the UK and grow really, really fast, have investor capital, have contracts, make money from patients and consumers.
transcript.zh: 人们自掏腰包支付高昂的费用。那里有私立连锁医院。一家数字医疗公司可以从英国去到美国并实现极快速的增长，获得投资资本、拿下合同，并从患者和消费者身上赚取利润。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: So digital kind of health progress in the US moves very quickly, but it's very siloed because the public system, Medicare, Medicaid, there's many inequalities, and many patients won't be able to access.
transcript.zh: 因此，美国在数字医疗方面的进展非常迅速，但极其孤立割裂，因为公共系统（Medicare 与 Medicaid）存在诸多不平等，许多患者根本无法获得这些服务。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And also, I think in the US, as well as in the UK, what we talked about earlier, which is the consumers' attitude towards technology and privacy and data sensitivity is very strong. And so happiness to share, although I guess we can caveat with they're happy to share with big tech companies, so I don't know.
transcript.zh: 而且我认为，在美国以及英国，就像我们之前讨论过的，消费者对科技、隐私和数据敏感性的态度非常坚决。因此对于数据共享的意愿——尽管我认为可以补充一点，他们倒是乐意同科技巨头分享，所以我也说不准。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Sure.
transcript.zh: 确实。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Maybe maybe we don't talk about that so much. It's difficult. I'm like I'm not the best expert at explaining the nuances.
transcript.zh: 或许我们不用在这上面花太多篇幅。这很难说清，我可能并不是阐释这些细微差别的最佳专家。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Ruby, thus far, you have given us two very good microcosmic representations of the whole societies. The UK, I'm not surprised, and the US, I'm not surprised at all to hear that you have very well-funded, very innovative digital health initiatives in the United States that find purchase, that find a large market, but that it's terribly unequal and that access is not...
transcript.zh: Ruby，到目前为止，你为我们提供了两个微缩版的全社会绝佳样本。英国的情况我不意外；而听到美国拥有资金极充沛、极具创新的数字医疗项目，并且找到了买家、打开了庞大市场，但我一点也不感到惊讶的是，它极其不平等，获取渠道也并不……

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So, let's move on to China, which is of course what we're most interested in for our purposes on this show. Tell me how things are going with digital healthcare in China. So you worked at AliHealth. They're one of the leaders, at the very forefront of this. What's it like in China at this point?
transcript.zh: 那么，我们来聊聊中国吧，这当然是本期节目最关注的核心。请跟我讲讲中国的数字医疗现状如何。你曾就职于阿里健康，他们是该领域的领军者之一，处于最前沿。目前中国的情况是怎样的？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah, in China, I would say it's probably the most mature digital health ecosystem in the world right now. That makes sense because every part of life is digital in China, so of course health is as well. Governance expects it, you know, the population expects it.
transcript.zh: 在中国，我认为它目前可能是全球最成熟的数字医疗生态系统。这完全说得通，因为在中国生活的方方面面都已实现数字化，医疗自然也不例外。政府治理有此预期，老百姓也有此预期。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: So if you order deliveries on your app, you access tools on your app, you do everything online through WeChat or whatever, then you would expect to be able to access health services as another type of service in your daily life, too, through digital means.
transcript.zh: 所以，如果你在 App 上点外卖、使用各种工具，通过微信等平台在网上处理一切事务，那么你自然也会期望能通过数字化手段，像获取日常生活中其他服务一样获取医疗服务。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Sure.
transcript.zh: 当然。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And so almost every physical health provider would likely have an online version, whether that's a smart hospital, internet clinic, cloud clinic, or otherwise.
transcript.zh: 因此，几乎每家实体医疗机构都可能有线上版本，无论是智慧医院、互联网诊所、云诊所还是其他形式。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And you can certainly book onto it, get results from it, even order your drugs on it and have them delivered to you very quickly and get your insurance from it, too.
transcript.zh: 你完全可以在上面挂号、查看检查结果，甚至在上面开药并极速送达，还能直接走医保结算。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So, so far, all of that sounds extremely reasonable and just simply added efficiencies, right, in the delivery of health services. But it goes beyond that.
transcript.zh: 到目前为止，所有这些听起来都极其顺理成章，只是在医疗服务提供过程中提升了效率，对吧？但它的意义远不止于此。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah.
transcript.zh: 是的。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: In China, so you have this situation where you have more than a thousand senior Chinese clinicians who have licensed digital versions of themselves, these digital avatars, to this company, again, affiliated with Alibaba, Ant-afu.
transcript.zh: 在中国，目前出现了一种情况：超过一千名中国资深临床医生将自己的数字分身、数字化身授权给了这家同样隶属于阿里巴巴体系的公司——蚂蚁阿福。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So these avatars are trained on their own, the clinician's own records and their own practice, and then patients consult with them directly. You have like virtual, I imagine, appointments with with these avatars.
transcript.zh: 这些数字分身利用医生自己的病历记录和临床经验进行训练，然后患者可以直接向他们问诊。我猜患者就像是和这些数字人进行线上预约看诊。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: And so you met a guy, a cardiologist, Dr. Li, who's in your book, and he's really gone all in on this, right? What's his reasoning? What actually happens in one of these consultations? Can you walk us through? I don't get a really clear sense of what that experience is like.
transcript.zh: 你在书里提到过你见过的一位心脏科医生李医生，他真的一头扎进了这套模式里，对吧？他的逻辑是什么？在这样的问诊中究竟会发生什么？你能带我们了解一下吗？我对那种就诊体验还没有特别清晰的画面感。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah, it's so interesting. So, Ant-afu, which is the hottest digital health app now in China, and that's an incredible feat because there've been many digital health apps in China for almost a decade now. But for this company to come in as a newbie and then win so quickly within about a year is because it's doing pretty innovative things.
transcript.zh: 对，这非常耐人寻味。蚂蚁阿福是目前中国最火的数字医疗 App。这确实是个不可思议的成就，因为数字医疗类 App 在中国已经存在近十年了。但这家公司作为后来者入局，却在一年左右的时间里迅速拔得头筹，原因在于他们做的事情极具创新性。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: So firstly, its strength is that it was built on China's fintech app, Ant Financial. And linking healthcare to money is what the secret is.
transcript.zh: 首先，它的核心优势在于它是构建在中国的金融科技应用——蚂蚁集团之上的。将医疗健康与支付端打通，这正是关键秘诀所在。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: When you have the insurance flow through, when you have capital and money there to solidify any health service, then that's kind of the only way it can succeed. Whereas you can have any type of digital health app anywhere, no matter the quality of service it provides, if there isn't a paying point, then how are you going to win? So I think that's kind of the secret sauce there.
transcript.zh: 一旦打通了医保或商保的资金流，有了资本和资金支撑去夯实各项医疗服务，这几乎是唯一能跑通的商业闭环。否则，你在任何地方做任何数字健康应用，无论服务质量多好，要是没有变现和支付节点，你拿什么胜出？所以我觉得这是他们的一大秘方。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: But then the other part that you just mentioned is so interesting. So Ant-afu, and it wasn't the first to do it, to try, but it's the first to do it at this scale and do it successfully, and do such successful PR around it, too.
transcript.zh: 但你刚才提到的另一点也极其有意思。蚂蚁阿福虽然不是第一个尝试这种模式的，但它是第一个把规模做到这么大、做得如此成功，并且品牌公关也打得极为响亮的一家。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: So successfully getting China's most senior expert, renowned doctors in any specialty to sign on, in some cases, upload their own patient records anonymized as evidence of their expertise and training and decision-making onto the platform.
transcript.zh: 他们成功吸引了中国各专科领域最顶尖、最权威的专家名医签约入驻，有些医生甚至将经过脱敏处理的真实病历上传到平台，作为体现其专业知识、临床训练与决策能力的训练数据。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Or other of these doctors, they might be doctor influencers, and then they upload their videos and content onto the app. It's kind of like diversed the data input they put onto the platform. But then they do that and allow AI avatar versions of themselves to be created and utilized on the platform.
transcript.zh: 另外一些医生本身可能是医学大 V，他们会把科普视频和内容上传到应用中。这使得输入平台的数据来源非常多元。他们在完成这些数据注入的同时，授权平台生成自己的 AI 数字人分身并投入运营。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So the AI has been trained on this corpus of their own clinical practice. Fascinating.
transcript.zh: 所以这个 AI 是用他们个人的临床实践语料库训练出来的。太有意思了。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah. And you can click through as a patient and consumer, you can click through to the AI chatbot doctor you want, and it'll come up with their photo, and their name, and you can talk to that AI bot who is the AI Dr. Li and get advice, which is...
transcript.zh: 是的。作为患者或用户，你可以点击进入你想咨询的 AI 聊天医生界面，上面会显示他们的照片和姓名，你可以直接与这位 AI 版的“李医生”对话并获取医疗建议，这……

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Are they specific to their expertise as much as possible? And I think conceptually that whole concept is incredible to many of us because, you know, as a doctor myself, I know that none of my colleagues in the UK would ever agree to something like this.
transcript.zh: 它们是否尽可能贴合医生的专业领域？我认为从概念上讲，这种模式对我们很多人来说简直难以置信。因为我自己就是医生，我知道我在英国的同行绝不可能同意这样的事情。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Would you?
transcript.zh: 你会同意吗？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: It's a good question. I, I perhaps would, and the reason is because I know that in reality the risks are so low. Because in some ways this whole endeavor is a massively successful PR strategy.
transcript.zh: 问得好。我……我也许会同意。原因在于，我知道实际上风险非常低。因为在某种程度上，这整套做法是一场极其成功的公关策略。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Because despite the risks that you can imagine, the regulations actually protect most of the risks. So in China, you cannot get an initial diagnosis or initial treatment scenario online. It always has to be in person with a real doctor.
transcript.zh: 因为尽管你能想象到种种风险，但监管规定实际上兜住了大部分隐患。在中国，你无法在网上完成初诊或初次治疗方案的制定，初诊必须由真人医生当面进行。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I see, I see. There are still hard limits drawn around.
transcript.zh: 明白了，懂了。周围依然划定了严格的红线。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah, hard limits. So from the patient's side, you get the perception of, you know, expertise from a specialist that you're paying for more. From the platform's point of view, you're making a lot more money and building your brand. But from the doctor's point of view, you're protected by, you know, ongoing regulatory mechanisms.
transcript.zh: 对，严格的红线。所以从患者的角度来看，你感受到了多花钱挂号的专家所提供的专业服务；从平台的角度来看，既赚到了更多钱，又打造了品牌；而从医生的角度来看，又有现行的监管机制提供保护。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: So it's really a glorified, you know, glorified ChatGPT, glorified DeepSeek with lower risks than you can imagine.
transcript.zh: 所以它本质上就是一个美化版的……美化版的ChatGPT，美化版的DeepSeek，其风险其实远比你想象的要低。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Okay, because I remember you talk about in your book a sleep specialist who is already seeing like 10,000 patients a year in person. That sounds like a lot to me. I don't know how it compares. But now he fields through his digital avatar on Ant Afu 3.7 million inquiries a year.
transcript.zh: 好的。因为我记得你在书中提到一位睡眠专科医生，他线下每年就已经要接诊大约一万名患者。这在我看来已经非常多了，我不太清楚横向对比如何。但现在，他通过在蚂蚁“安阿福”上的数字分身，每年要处理370万次问询。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So these are just inquiries. These are digital interactions that could be taking place simultaneously. They don't need to be in sequence, right? These are, though, inquiries. They're not actual consultations. He cannot then go and diagnose somebody with apnea and says, you need, you know, to get a CPAP or something like that, right?
transcript.zh: 所以这些仅仅是问询。这些是数字化交互，可以同时并发进行，不需要按顺序一个一个来，对吧？但这些终究只是问询，并不是真正的诊疗。他不能凭此去诊断某人患有呼吸暂停综合征，并说“你需要配一台睡眠呼吸机（CPAP）”之类的，对吧？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: No.
transcript.zh: 不行。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: He's not able to issue, for example, prescriptions. I mean, I know that in China it's pretty easy to get a prescription for non-prescription medicines, just even through Meituan, right?
transcript.zh: 比如，他无法开具处方。我的意思是，我知道在中国想开非处方药的方子其实相当容易，甚至直接通过美团就可以，对吧？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah.
transcript.zh: 是的。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I can go onto a pharmacy and answer a couple of questions, and even for a medicine I know is a prescription-only medicine, they will often just simply issue it right there, just after you've answered a couple of simple questions. It's unbelievable, but I worry about that. This is why there are too many antibiotics out there in China.
transcript.zh: 我可以进一家药店回答几个问题，甚至有些我知道明确属于处方药的药品，只要你回答几个简单的问题，他们往往当场就能直接开出来。这真是不可思议，但我挺担心的。这也是为什么中国抗生素滥用比较严重的原因。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yes. Yes.
transcript.zh: 是的。没错。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Yeah, anyway, that's interesting. I need to try this thing out. I need to get on and interact on Ant Afu with a... that'll be really interesting. I wonder if patients can keep up with this, though. I mean, because, you know, there are...
transcript.zh: 好吧，总之这挺有意思的。我得亲自试用一下这东西。我得上去在蚂蚁“安阿福”上互动一下……那肯定很有趣。不过我在想，患者能不能跟得上这种节奏？因为你知道……

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: 20 million people in China over 60 we were talking about, right? And by your own account, fewer than half of these can actually use these platforms independently. I mean, your grandmother still calls London to be talked through the prompts, right?
transcript.zh: 我们刚才提到，中国有2000多万60岁以上的人口，对吧？而且据你所说，其中能独立使用这些平台的还不到一半。我是说，你奶奶至今还得给远在伦敦的你打电话，让你一步步指导她怎么操作，对吧？

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: What does it mean to build this sort of a system for an aging population when the aging population can't necessarily operate it very well? I mean, we've all had that experience of helping aging relatives. Can they keep up?
transcript.zh: 如果老年群体本身并不能很好地操作这些系统，那么为老龄化人口构建这样一套体系又意味着什么呢？我们都有过帮家里老人捣鼓电子设备的经历。他们跟得上吗？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: I don't know, that's my answer. Digital literacy is a huge issue. We can generally say China's silver population are maybe a tiny bit more digitally savvy than in many other countries, because they've had to be, that's the way life is.
transcript.zh: 我的回答是：我不知道。数字素养是个巨大的难题。我们大体可以说，中国的“银发族”可能比很多其他国家的老人稍微懂一点数字科技，因为生活所迫，他们不得不学着去用。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Except my in-laws. Yeah, they're not. They're terrible. Yeah, they cause my blood pressure to rise every time I get a tech help question. Anyway...
transcript.zh: 我岳父母可除外。是的，他们完全不行，糟糕透顶。每次他们发消息让我帮忙解决技术问题，我的血压都蹭蹭往上涨。不过言归正传……

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yes, definitely. Broadly speaking, technology is creating new challenges, creating new inequalities in health service access and delivery, which is a massive policy and system challenge. So what can be done? It's difficult to say.
transcript.zh: 确实如此。概括来说，技术在带来便利的同时也在制造新的挑战，在医疗服务的获取和交付上拉开新的不平等差距，这是政策和体制层面面临的巨大课题。那该怎么办呢？现在很难下定论。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: At the moment, as I anecdotally wrote about, and as your experience with your in-laws, you're probably the one helping them out, clicking on the right buttons on their phone. It's very labor-intensive for the family. What's going to happen later on?
transcript.zh: 目前来看，就像我书里记录的亲身经历，以及你帮岳父母的经历一样，通常得靠家人出手相助，在手机上帮他们点选正确的按键。这对家庭来说是极耗费精力的负担。未来会怎样呢？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Maybe we can see the market moving to address these issues, seeing them as an opportunity, creating elder-friendly tools, at-home care robots that do basic tasks and help out rather than, you know, assuming that the user can follow technical instructions.
transcript.zh: 或许我们会看到市场逐步转向并解决这些痛点，将其视为商机——去开发适老化工具，或是能够分担基础任务的居家看护机器人，而不是默认用户都能看懂复杂的技术操作指引。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: But overall, the trend is that much of the population is using technology to access healthcare, and so in China scale often overrides and takes up much of the attention, rather than those lagging behind, and it's always really hard to cover and ensure that smaller proportion is taken care of. It's a good question.
transcript.zh: 但总的趋势是，大部分人口都在利用科技手段获取医疗服务。因此在中国，宏大的整体规模往往会掩盖个体的困境，吸走绝大部分关注，而那些掉队的人往往被忽视。要做到全面覆盖、确保少数群体得到照料，始终是一件极具挑战的事。这是一个非常深刻的问题。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So, I want to bring this back to you personally here, because you talk about in your book how your parents actually tried to talk you out of practicing medicine. They told you that it meant a whole lifetime of eating bitterness.
transcript.zh: 我想把话题拉回到你个人身上。你在书中提到，你的父母当年其实极力劝阻你学医，他们告诉你，行医就意味着要“吃一辈子的苦”。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: And you have in your book a character who you call Dr. Wang, who has the same surname as you, she's about the same age, the same height if I remember correctly. And she's sort of like your own alter ego, sort of like "there, but for the grace of God, go I." Somebody who is in medicine, she's an internist at a large Guangzhou public hospital.
transcript.zh: 你在书中描写了一位被称为“王医生”的人物，她和你同姓，年纪差不多，如果我没记错的话连身高都相仿。她就像是另一个你，一种“若非命运眷顾，我也可能如此”的镜像写照——一个真正在中国行医的人，她是广州一家大型公立医院的内科医生。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Tell me about her and her experience and what that told you about the practice of medicine in China today.
transcript.zh: 跟我讲讲她和她的经历吧，从她的身上，你看到了当今中国行医现状的哪些侧面？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah, my parents didn't want me to become a doctor because what they know about doctors in China, since they grew up and lived there, was that it's sort of a terrible life: low wages, lack of respect, long hours, burnout, and really, you know, as you said, sacrificing on behalf of others, not really living life for yourself.
transcript.zh: 是的，我父母以前不希望我学医。因为他们在中国土生土长，在他们的认知里，当医生日子过得很苦：收入低、缺乏社会尊重、工作时间长、极度职业倦怠，而且真如你所说，完全是在为别人牺牲，根本没有属于自己的生活。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: I think that's been the case for many decades because of the way the system could not help its workers in their welfare, in their in their professions. And it's perhaps improving, you know, with policy reform, with the role of technology, of course, but it still persists in in many ways.
transcript.zh: 我认为这种情况已经持续了几十年，体制在保障医护人员福祉和职业发展方面一直力不从心。当然，随着政策改革和科技的应用，情况或许在改善，但在许多方面这一困境依然存在。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: So I wrote about Dr. Wang in Guangzhou, who I met when I was doing a research project there. And you know, as I wrote about, we I found many similarities personally with her, which was why I empathized so much. I was imagining myself in her place.
transcript.zh: 我在书中写到了广州的王医生，那是我在那边做一个研究项目时认识的。正如我在书中所写的，我发现自己在个人层面上和她有许多相似之处，这也是为什么我深感共情，总会设身处地代入她的处境。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And the burnout impacted her so much so that she ended up having a miscarriage, which is, you know, is such an awful tragedy. I wrote about her sacrificing her personal life for the benefit of patients. She went back to work the next day.
transcript.zh: 高强度的过劳对她造成了极大伤害，以至于她最后不幸流产，这是一场可怕的悲剧。我写下了她为了病人如何牺牲自己的个人生活：流产后第二天她就重返了工作岗位。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And she was such a resilient—she is such a resilient, strong person. It was very inspirational. And it made me think back to my times, especially training as a junior doctor, resident doctor in the UK. How, you know, we've all had sleepless nights, night shifts, no time to eat, on your feet all day. But being a doctor in China really takes it to the next level.
transcript.zh: 她是如此有韧性、坚强的一个人，令人非常钦佩。这也让我回想起了自己在英国作为初级医生、住院医师接受培训的岁月。我们都经历过彻夜不眠、连轴夜班、顾不上吃饭、整天脚不沾地，但在中国当医生，那种辛苦程度真的是更上一层楼。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Earlier, Kaiser, you were talking about the waiting list in hospital. You know, having one minute to perhaps see a doctor and then having someone else behind you queue up in a public health hospital in China. So these doctors in China, they're seeing hundreds of patients a day. And that volume and that pressure is really difficult.
transcript.zh: 刚才 Kaiser 你提到医院里的排队现象，在中国公立医院，看病往往只有一分钟时间，身后还紧挨着排队的下一位患者。中国的医生一天要看上百个病人。那种接诊量和心理压力，是非常难以承受的。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And not only creates problems for the doctor and for the patient, too, in terms of quality of care, but also creates relationship, communication breakdown. And so in the book, I talked about doctor violence, too, as this awful phenomenon.
transcript.zh: 这不仅给医生带来负担，也影响了患者的就医质量，更导致了医患沟通的断裂与关系恶化。因此在书中，我也讨论了暴力伤医这一极其恶劣的现象。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Yeah, yīnào, medical disturbances, yeah.
transcript.zh: 对，医闹。所谓“医疗纠纷滋事”。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah. I wonder if you have any stories from your time in China.
transcript.zh: 是的。不知道你在中国生活时，有没有听说过类似的事情？

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I haven't experienced it, or I haven't perpetrated it or experienced it myself, but it's common enough, you know, that we all know what this means when somebody says yīnào in China. I mean, I think in your book, you talk about 80% of medical professionals report having first-hand experience with workplace violence.
transcript.zh: 我自己倒没有亲历过，既没参与过也没碰上过。但在中国“医闹”这个词非常普遍，大家都心知肚明是什么意思。你在书中提到，有80%的医务人员自称亲身遭遇过职场暴力。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I mean, you have in, again in your, you describe how a hospital in Shenzhen put staff actually in body armor with helmets for ward rounds. I mean, how did the relationship get this bad? I mean,
transcript.zh: 而且你还在书中描述过，深圳一家医院的医护人员甚至要穿防弹衣、戴头盔去查房。医患关系怎么会恶化到如此地步？

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: It's the doctors, look, medicine used to be a very prestigious career in China, right? It's now like one of the least popular subjects at the top universities. I mean, this is not unrelated to what's happening with this violence.
transcript.zh: 医生……你看，学医在中国曾经是一门非常受人尊重的职业，对吧？现在它却成了顶尖高校中最不受欢迎的专业之一。我觉得这跟这种暴力事件频发并非毫无关联。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I mean, I don't want to leave this only on the grim side, because you know, I think there's been a lot of things that have improved life for clinicians, like this technology thing. I can imagine that somebody like your sleep specialist now is sleeping a little better. They're not necessarily having to see quite as many patients because their digital avatar is taking some of the workload off of them. I would hope that would be one of the effects of it, but tell me about that.
transcript.zh: 不过我也不想只停留在灰暗的一面，因为我觉得很多技术手段确实改善了临床医生的处境。比如科技赋能，我能想象像你提到的那位睡眠专家现在应该睡得稍微踏实些了。他们不一定非得看那么多病人，因为数字分身替他们分担了一部分工作负荷。我希望这能成为其积极影响之一，你能多聊聊这方面吗？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah, I wrote about doctor violence and these phenomena occurring because patients and doctors don't have enough time to build a relationship, to build trust, and build understanding because medicine is such a vulnerable place. Being sick is so vulnerable, being unwell is to be very vulnerable.
transcript.zh: 是的，我在书里写到涉医暴力以及这些现象的发生，很大程度上是因为医患之间没有足够的时间建立关系、信任和相互理解。因为医疗关乎最脆弱的时刻，生病是人最脆弱的时候，身体抱恙会让人感到无依无靠。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Indeed, yeah. And so in those situations where you don't have enough time with your doctor, when they might be too tired to say an extra word of comfort, then oftentimes you can imagine trust breaks down.
transcript.zh: 确实如此。在那种情况下，你和医生接触的时间极短，而他们可能已经累得连一句宽慰的话都说不出来了，往往在这个时候，信任就会瓦解。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And then the system itself propagates, because there's no clear mechanism of responsibility and accountability. Everyone just keeps going, moves on to the next, and as the family member, perhaps you really want someone to explain, you want someone to blame.
transcript.zh: 接着这种机制会不断恶性蔓延，因为缺乏清晰的问责和追责渠道。所有人都在硬撑，紧接着看下一个病人；而作为患者家属，你可能极度渴望有人给个说法，甚至想找人泄愤。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And it can come out to this awful scenario of violence against doctors, even murder against doctors that we've seen in China, leading to the protective mechanisms. We've seen photos of doctors with helmets and bats and things to protect themselves. It's really incredible what it came to be.
transcript.zh: 这就可能激化为极端的暴力伤医，甚至是我们在中国见过的弑医惨案，以至于催生了各种防御手段。我们都见过医生戴着头盔、拿着钢叉或球棒防身的照片，演变成这种地步真是令人匪夷所思。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: I think as you said, it's getting better, and I wrote about it in this book because I wanted to think about the role of technology in all of this. Hopefully, improving efficiency, improving access to healthcare, so that the burdens of numbers of patients seeing healthcare professionals can be reduced or streamlined in certain ways.
transcript.zh: 我觉得正如你所说，情况正在好转。我在书中着墨这一点，是想探讨技术在其中能扮演什么角色。它有望提高效率、扩大医疗服务的可及性，从而在一定程度上减轻医护人员接诊海量病患的负荷，或是优化就医流程。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: But of course, technology is also adding new time burdens. A doctor is not trained in IT, not trained to use an app. If they've got, as you said, the sleep specialist having so many more patients channeled through to them via the platform because patients are allowed more efficient access to the doctor, then that means they have even more patients to see and to treat, and also they have more digital paperwork to do.
transcript.zh: 但当然，科技也在带来新的时间负担。医生并不是搞IT的，也没受过专门使用各种App的训练。如果就像你说的，那位睡眠专家通过平台导流来了多得多的患者——因为患者能更便捷地联系到医生——那就意味着他们要看诊和治疗的病人反而更多了，而且还得应付更多的数字化文书工作。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: ...instead of actually seeing patients.
transcript.zh: ……而不是真正在看病人。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Yeah, I remember you actually talk about how he's got two phones and a desktop, and he's between chat windows and charts. It's like, I don't know whether his life has gotten easier or harder at this point.
transcript.zh: 是的，我记得你还写到他手里拿着两部手机，面前摆着台式机，在各种聊天窗口和病历表之间反复横跳。我真不知道眼下他的生活到底是变轻松了还是更难了。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah. Easier or harder, yeah.
transcript.zh: 是啊。变轻松了还是更难了，确实。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Yeah, yeah. So listen, there's still all sorts that I'd love to talk to you about. I mean, we haven't even really touched on sort of the Chinese healthcare system and the rest of the world.
transcript.zh: 对，对。话说回来，我还有很多方面特别想和你聊。比如我们都还没来得及真正探讨中国医疗体系与世界其他地区的关系。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: But maybe we'll leave something for another conversation another time, because I have kept you for a very long time and you are a very, very busy person. But what a fantastic thing. I mean, before we get to recommendations, let me just say, who is somebody who's doing work on China, health-related ideally, who we should also be reading?
transcript.zh: 不过也许我们可以把这些留到下次再聊，因为我已经占用了你很长时间，而你又非常非常忙。但这期内容真的太棒了。在进入推荐环节之前我想先问问，在研究中国领域——最好是医疗健康相关的——还有哪些人的作品是我们应该拜读的？

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I mean, is there somebody else writing a good healthcare Substack on China, some younger colleague of yours maybe, somebody who you know through your time at Schwarzman who you think we should be paying attention to for our paying-it-forward section?
transcript.zh: 比如有没有其他人在写关于中国医疗的高质量 Substack 专栏？或者是你的某位年轻同事，比如你在苏世民学者项目认识的、值得我们在“后浪推荐”环节关注的人？

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: I think for the health world and China, someone I respect so much and, you know, learn from so much is Professor Yanzhong Huang. He's a professor at Schwarzman Scholars, but also a professor at Seton University and at the Council on Foreign Relations.
transcript.zh: 我觉得在医疗健康与中国这个领域，有一位我极其尊敬并深感受益匪浅的学者，那就是黄严忠教授。他是苏世民学者项目的教授，同时也是西顿大学教授以及美国外交关系协会（CFR）的专家。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Yes, yeah. He was I think the first person I had on the show right after the COVID epidemic broke out.
transcript.zh: 对，是的。我记得新冠疫情刚爆发后，我请上节目的第一位嘉宾就是他。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Right. Yeah, his expertise is on the geopolitics of China and healthcare. So I really, you know, always follow his work.
transcript.zh: 没错。他的专业专长在于中国与医疗健康的地缘政治学。所以我一直非常密切地关注他的研究。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: But I think there are also really great people working on non-health topics that I take a lot of inspiration from. I wanted to mention Afra Wang, who's a writer and journalist. She writes at the Concurrent newsletter.
transcript.zh: 但我觉得在非医疗领域，也有很多非常优秀的人，给了我很多启发。我想提一下王磬（Afra Wang），她是一位作家兼记者。她主笔《不合时宜》（The Concurrent）通讯专栏。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Oh, yeah. Wonderful writer, really. Wonderful, wonderful.
transcript.zh: 噢，对。极具才华的写作者，真的非常出色。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And a bit similar to how we were talking about the way culture impacts everything, including healthcare, the way she covers the cultural parts of technology and kind of the deeper comparisons with the rest of the world, thinking about human choices and incentives. So it's very thought-provoking for me to then take it to the health tech angle.
transcript.zh: 这有点像我们刚才聊到的，文化如何深刻影响包括医疗在内的一切。她对科技背后的文化层面以及与世界其他地区的深度对比有着独到观察，思考人的选择与激励机制。这对我从医疗科技角度进行延伸思考非常有启发性。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: And then finally, also Olivia Plotnick, who's another Substacker too. She's based in Shanghai, does very interesting, like, on-the-ground work. I think she visited like 30 cities across China, especially the lower-tier cities.
transcript.zh: 最后还有 Olivia Plotnick，她也是一位 Substack 创作者。她常驻上海，做非常扎实的田野调查式一线研究。她走访了中国大约三十座城市，尤其是下沉市场与低线城市。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: She looks at branding, you know, including health and wellness, but across kind of consumer behavior. And again, I think that's very relevant for me and my work on health.
transcript.zh: 她主要研究品牌塑造，涵盖大健康及各类消费行为。我觉得这对我以及我的健康领域研究非常有参考价值。

transcript.speaker: Dr. Ruby Wang
transcript.en: It's about the way China's changing, society's changing, how people are choosing, the way soft power impacts, you know, Chinese perspectives.
transcript.zh: 它关乎中国的变迁、社会的转型、人们的消费抉择，以及软实力如何深刻影响中国人的视角与观念。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: options of the world, of how they use technology. Um, and I think she's really excellent at that. So lots of recommendations for people.
transcript.zh: 放眼全球视角去审视他们如何运用技术。我认为她在这方面非常出色。所以我为大家推荐了很多人。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Yeah, three great ones. I mean, Dr. Yanzhong Huang, of course. I think he's very well known, and, you know, he's, I follow him on Twitter, read a lot of his stuff. Of course, hardly somebody who needs more attention. I think he's the go-to guy for most people on public health policy when it comes to China.
transcript.zh: 是的，这三个推荐都很棒。黄严忠博士当然不用说，他知名度极高，我在推特上关注了他，也读过很多他的文章。他当然已经名声在外，无需额外引流了，我认为对大多数人来说，只要谈及中国的公共卫生政策，他都是首选权威专家。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: And then, of course, Afra, who has been on the show as well. She's wonderful. When she came on to talk about a big piece she did for Wired magazine, which I would still love to talk to her more about because it's just fascinating. Yeah, and then Olivia Plotnick, who I've been in touch with, and I would love to actually have on the program as well.
transcript.zh: 当然还有王磬（Afra），她也上过我们的节目。她太棒了。当时她来聊了自己为《连线》（Wired）杂志写的一篇重磅报道，我其实还想找机会和她多聊聊，因为那篇报道确实引人入胜。还有 Olivia Plotnick，我也一直和她保持着联系，非常希望能邀请她上节目。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Fantastic. Thank you, Ruby. Now, what about for just good old recommendations? Is there a novel you've read, or a book, or anything that you've got for listeners?
transcript.zh: 太棒了，谢谢你，Ruby。那么在常规的内容推荐环节，你读过什么小说、书籍或其他作品想分享给听众吗？

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yeah. So, I wanted to recommend Professor Arthur Kleinman, um, who wrote Deep China: The Moral Life of the Person. So you can tell my theme is culture and anthropology, and how that relates to healthcare.
transcript.zh: 有的。我想推荐 Arthur Kleinman（凯博文）教授，他写了《深访中国：个体道德生活》（Deep China: The Moral Life of the Person）。你肯定看出来了，我的主题始终是文化与人类学，以及它们如何与医疗卫生相关联。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: So that book is all about what being sick reveals about society and culture in China. So like psychiatry, caregiving, as China's changed socially, how its patients and families have evolved with the times, you know.
transcript.zh: 那本书全方位探讨了“生病”这件事折射出的中国社会与文化。例如精神医学、照护问题；随着中国社会的变迁，患者和家庭如何随时代演进。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: As a country develops so quickly, how the family structures change, how that impacted illness and suffering. And it's an academic book, and different chapters are led by different groups.
transcript.zh: 随着国家如此迅猛地发展，家庭结构如何演变，这又如何影响了疾病与痛苦的体验。这是一本学术著作，不同的章节由不同的学者团队主笔。

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: But Professor Arthur Kleinman, who is based in Boston at Harvard, is, you know, so wonderful. I'm a huge fan of all of his work. He wrote another book called...
transcript.zh: 但在哈佛大学波士顿校区的 Arthur Kleinman 教授确实太杰出了。我是他所有作品的忠实粉丝。他还写过另一本书叫……

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I'm going to buy this right now. It looks fantastic. Buying it on Kindle right now. Fantastic recommendation.
transcript.zh: 我马上就去买这本书。看起来太精彩了，我现在就在 Kindle 上下单。极力推荐！

transcript.speaker: Ruby Wang
transcript.en: Yes, it's really excellent, very thought-provoking. So that would be my recommendation.
transcript.zh: 是的，非常精彩，发人深省。这就是我的推荐。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: All right. I am going to recommend a couple of things. Mine, first, is a novel this week, John Williams' novel, Augustus.
transcript.zh: 好的。我打算推荐两样东西。首先是本周的一部小说，John Williams 的《奥古斯都》（Augustus）。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: I recommended John Williams' book, Butcher's Crossing, on the show not that very long ago. And a lot of people know him now for his novel, Stoner, which had a strange kind of second life as a rediscovered masterpiece, like 50 years after it came out.
transcript.zh: 不久前我才在节目里推荐过 John Williams 的《屠夫十字镇》（Butcher's Crossing）。现在很多人熟知他，是因为他的小说《斯通纳》（Stoner），那本书在出版约 50 年后奇迹般重获新生，被重新发现为传世杰作。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: Augustus is the third novel of his now that I'm recommending. It won the National Book Award. Actually, it won it in combination with another—there was somebody else who won it as well that same year, which was the first time the National Book Award was given to two people.
transcript.zh: 《奥古斯都》是我推荐他的第三部小说了。它曾斩获美国国家图书奖。实际上，那一年是与另一部作品共享该奖项，那是国家图书奖历史上首次将奖项同时颁给两位作者。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: It's an epistolary novel about, you know, the Roman Emperor Augustus, Octavian, who of course is known as Augustus. It's told entirely through a crazy quilt of letters and little fragments, letters of...
transcript.zh: 这是一部书信体小说，讲述的是罗马皇帝奥古斯都——也就是大家熟知的屋大维。全书完全由一幅由书信与零散片段拼贴而成的复杂画卷铺展开来，信件包括……

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: ...from people who you would expect, like his family members and his close friends like Agrippa, but also from poets and playwrights of the time. Virgil is in there, and Strabo, and Horace, and all these other people.
transcript.zh: ……信件既来自那些你意料之中的人，比如他的家人和他像阿格里帕（Agrippa）这样的挚友；但也有来自当时的诗人和剧作家。维吉尔（Virgil）就在其中，还有斯特拉波（Strabo）、贺拉斯（Horace）以及所有其他人。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: And it's amazing just how Williams is able to give these people such different voices. That's the thing that really amazes me about this guy, is his range. So, you know, you have this kind of quiet campus novel in Stoner about a very undistinguished, very normal English professor.
transcript.zh: 令人惊叹的是，Williams 居然能赋予这些人如此迥异的声音。这个作家真正让我折服的地方，正是他创作跨度之广。你看，他在《斯通纳》（Stoner）里写了一部克制内敛的校园小说，讲的是一位默默无闻、极为普通的英语教授。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: And then you have this kind of anti-Western about buffalo hunters in Kansas. And now, you know, this novel about imperial Rome, and each one is really just so assured, and so completely different in subject, in tone, in structure.
transcript.zh: 然后他又写了一部关于堪萨斯州猎水牛人的反西部题材小说；如今又是这本关于罗马帝国的小说。每一部都驾轻就熟，在题材、语调和结构上完全不同。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: And somehow he does all of this without really kind of showing off. It's just the language is... there's so much restraint in the way he writes, it's just really admirable.
transcript.zh: 而且不知怎么的，他做到了这一切，却毫无炫技之感。他的文字……他写作的那种极度克制，实在令人钦佩。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
transcript.en: So if you've read Stoner, as many of you have, and wondered whether John Williams had anything else up his sleeve, the answer is yes, and it is Augustus, so check that out. And I want to make one more quick recommendation.
transcript.zh: 所以，如果你们很多人一样读过《斯通纳》，并好奇 John Williams 是否还有别的压箱之作，答案是肯定的，那就是《奥古斯都》（Augustus），大家不妨找来看看。另外我还想快速做个推荐。

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo

transcript.speaker: Kaiser Kuo
